text:
Regina v. Lelas

Indexed as: R. v. Lelas

(C.A.)

74 O.R. (2d) 552

[1990] O.J. No. 1587

Action No. 347/90

ONTARIO

Court of Appeal

Houlden, Carthy and Galligan JJ.A.

August 31, 1990.

Criminal law -- Sentence -- Property offences -- Mischief -- Accused pleading guilty to three charges, involving anti- semitic spray painting on synagogue and other property, resulting in extreme distress to members of congregation -- Six months' imprisonment with two years probation inadequate -- One year sentence substituted.
The accused, who was a member of the Ku Klux Klan and described himself as a racist, together with one companion, spray painted anti-semitic symbols and slogans, many connected with Nazism, on and near a synagogue, on a Hebrew school building and on an automobile. He was charged with mischief to property over $1,000. At trial, the accused showed remorse, admitted that his acts were idiotic, and made an apology. The trial judge noted the distress caused to the Jewish community, particularly to the members of the synagogue congregation, many of whom had survived the Holocaust, and to participants in a wedding scheduled at the synagogue the following day (before the paint could be removed). He also noted mitigating factors, including the facts that further distress to the Jewish community was saved by the accused's guilty plea, that the accused otherwise appeared to be responsible and co-operative and that the offences were spontaneous, unplanned and unsophisticated, and were not committed at the instigation of any racist group, in spite of the accused's membership in such groups. Sentences on the three charges of six months concurrent were imposed, with two years' probation, one term of which was restitution. The Crown sought leave to appeal, and if granted, appealed against sentence.
Held, leave to appeal should be granted and the appeal should be allowed.
Per Houlden J.A. (Carthy J.A. concurring): The desecration of a place of worship, whatever the faith, was a serious matter, particularly where such desecration was intended to cause emotional damage to members of the congregation. The accused had admitted wishing to enrage the Jewish community. Such acts went beyond the mere intent to damage property. Mischief which is racially or religiously motivated and done to cause emotional injury to a particular segment of society required a far more severe penalty than mischief done merely to damage property. Although the mitigating factors considered by the trial judge were properly regarded as relevant, they did not justify a six-month sentence, and one year's imprisonment should be substituted on each charge, to be served concurrently. The probation order was affirmed.
Per Galligan J.A. (dissenting): Although the beliefs of the accused were repugnant, he should not be punished for them, and the sentence should not appear to do so. The trial judge properly considered all the mitigating and aggravating factors. The sentence imposed was based on a fair balance between those factors, and was not shown to be unfit.
APPLICATION for leave to appeal and appeal against sentence.

Cases referred to
R. v. Ingram and Grimsdale (1977),
1977 CanLII 2018 (ON CA)
, 35 C.C.C. (2d) 376 (Ont. C.A.)

Jamie C. Klukach, for the Crown, appellant.
Peter V. DeJulio, for respondent.

HOULDEN J.A. (CARTHY J.A. concurring):-- On January 12, 1990,
the respondent Zvonimir Lelas (Lelas) pleaded guilty before
Provincial Court judge Scullion to three charges of mischief to
property, the value of which exceeded $1,000. On March 12,
1990, he was sentenced by His Honour Judge Scullion to six
months' imprisonment concurrent on each charge together with
two years' probation. The Crown applies for leave to appeal
sentence, and if leave is granted, asks that the appeal be
allowed and the sentence increased. I would grant leave to
appeal.

On Saturday evening, June 10, 1989, Lelas went to the home of
a friend, Elizabeth Major, to attend a barbecue. Three other
persons were also present. Lelas brought some alcohol with him,
and one of the others brought some L.S.D. During the course of
the evening, Lelas consumed some beer and had two hits of
L.S.D. Lelas did not, however, blame his use of alcohol and
drugs for his actions on that evening.

During the course of the evening, it was suggested that the
group would go to a synagogue for the purpose of spraying it
with paint. By the use of the yellow pages in the telephone
book, one of the group, not Lelas, located a nearby synagogue,
the Shaarei Shomayim Synagogue, at 470 Glencairn Avenue.

Lelas and one of his female companions obtained cans of spray
paint. Lelas used the paint to spray-paint two swastikas
circled in red on the door of the synagogue. He also painted
"Smash the Zog" on the sidewalk. "Zog" is an acronym for
"Zionist Occupational Government", an anti-semitic term. His
companion sprayed "WP" on the sides of the synagogue, "WP"
being an abbreviation for "White Power". Other slogans of a
similar nature were also sprayed on the synagogue property.

The group left the synagogue and while returning to the Major
home came upon a Hebrew school, the Yeshiva Yesodei Hatorah, at
77 Glenrush Boulevard. Lelas spray-painted "Nazism" and a
swastika on the school sign, and the words "The Wind is blown"
with a Celtic cross beside it and "Zog has died" on the door of
the school. There was no evidence that Lelas' companions
participated in the spray painting at the school.

Finally, outside of 14 Glenrush Boulevard, Lelas spray-
painted a swastika on the hood of an automobile owned by
Nattan Fichman.

The cost of repairing the damage to the synagogue was $1,035
and to the school $200. The paint on the automobile was removed
without cost, but the trial judge found that the damage to the
automobile was about $200. It was conceded that the automobile
and the two buildings each had a value in excess of $1,000. As
a term of the probation order, Judge Scullion ordered Lelas to
pay restitution of $1,435 to the victims.

There was a great amount of media attention given to the
incident. This was not confined to the Toronto area, but
extended right across Canada.

Lelas was arrested 20 days after the event. At the time of
his arrest he was found in possession of three Nazi flags, a
framed photograph of Adolf Hitler, a framed membership in the
Ku Klux Klan and a Ku Klux Klan robe.

Lelas' parents were both born in Yugoslavia but met and
married in Australia. They immigrated to Canada in 1969 when
the respondent was two years of age. At the time of sentencing,
Lelas was residing with his parents. He has a Grade 12
education and has been employed off and on for five years by
his father as a dry wall installer. He is described by his
mother in the pre-sentence report as "a hard and reliable
worker". At the time of sentencing, he was 22 years of age.
According to the pre-sentence report, he is bright and
articulate.

In 1986, Lelas was convicted of theft under $200 and given an
absolute discharge. Later in the same year, he was convicted of
assault causing bodily harm and sentenced to five months. When
he was on parole on the assault charge, he conducted himself
properly.

Since the age of 17 or 18, Lelas has been involved in various
"white supremist groups". He was suspended from school on
one occasion for having swastikas depicted in his locker. In
the summer of 1988, he began attending meetings of the
"Nationalist Party of Canada", a Toronto-based white
supremist group. He described himself as being a "racist'', in
that he respects all races and believes that each race should
have a distinct homeland. He has closely followed the teachings
of Ernst Zundel and subscribes to the belief that the magnitude
of the Holocaust is a Zionist hoax.

The author of the pre-sentence report states:

The subject describes himself as a "National Socialist" and
dislikes being referred to [as] a "Nazi" or "Neo-Nazi". He
maintains that he only resorts to using Nazi symbolism as it
is a way of enraging the Jewish community. The subject enjoys
collecting Nazi paraphernalia and books which support his
point of view.

(Emphasis added)

In 1988, Lelas became actively involved with the Ku Klux Klan
and in January 1989 he was sworn in as a member of the Klan. He
has since risen to the highest ranking position in that
organization in Ontario: "Exalted Cyclops". In this position,
he is primarily responsible for the screening and
indoctrination of new members. There was no evidence that these
offences were committed at the instigation of or in collusion
with the Ku Klux Klan.

When apprehended, Lelas was co-operative with the police and
signed a written statement in which he admitted his involvement
in the offences. In that statement he described his actions as
follows:

It was an idiotic move on my behalf which was meaningless.
I'm sorry I did it. I wanted to get attention from my friends
and show off.

During the sentencing hearing, Lelas apologized "to the Jewish
community and any other ethnic groups" offended by his actions.
His Honour Judge Scullion found that Lelas had demonstrated
some remorse through his apology and plea of guilty.

Mr. Benny Stark, house chairman of the Shaarei Shomayim
Synagogue, testified at the sentencing hearing concerning the
effect of the offence on the members of the congregation. He
gave evidence that of the 1,400 members of the congregation, at
least 65 to 70 per cent are Holocaust survivors. On the morning
following the commission of the offence, Mr. Stark went to the
synagogue to survey the damage. When he arrived, he saw a group
of people who had attended the synagogue to worship and who
were very upset. Mr. Stark, himself a survivor of the
Holocaust, described his reaction as follows:

I don't have to tell you how much I was personally,
emotionally hurt as a survivor to see after 45 years that
horrible thing on our synagogue ...

Mr. Stark further testified that a wedding had been scheduled
for the synagogue for that afternoon. He telephoned the mother
of the bride and told her what had happened. The bride's
mother, also a Holocaust survivor, reacted with great upset and
distress. Later that day, Mr. Stark saw the family involved in
the wedding. "Instead of happiness," Mr. Stark testified,
"there was crying".

The Canadian Jewish Congress represents the Jewish community
in Canada. Almost every synagogue or Jewish organization in
Canada is a member of the Congress. Mr. Bernard Farber, the
research director on community relations for the Canadian
Jewish Congress, also gave evidence at the sentencing hearing.
It was part of Mr. Farber's duties to monitor anti-semitic
activity in Canada. Mr. Farber said that the reaction of the
Jewish community to Lelas' actions were the strongest he had
seen during the five years that he had been connected with the
Congress. The reaction varied from "absolute fear to outrage".
According to Mr. Farber, most of the S.S. guards in the
concentration camps wore the insignia of the swastika encircled
in red. This was the kind of swastika that Lelas sprayed on the
Shaarei Shomayim Synagogue. Mr. Farber testified that it
brought back visions to the Holocaust survivors of the S.S.
guards in the concentration camps. In describing the impact of
the spray painting, Mr. Farber testified:

So, one can understand then that anyone approaching a
synagogue, anyone seeing this in the media would have an
immediate emotional type of reaction. Some people that I
spoke to directly indicated that it's this type of thing that
they feared the most after the holocaust and coming to Canada
was the manifestations of anti-Semitism and manifestations of
neo-Nazis and the fear of its recurrence, even if it may not
be correct, that fear was so present and so much a part of
their concern that we couldn't help but hear it again not
only in terms of Toronto, but certainly from various
communities across the country.

After the incident of June 10, 1989, there was an outbreak of
daubing of swastikas on synagogues. Within a three to five-week
period, Mr. Farber said, there was a swastika daubing in
Ottawa, Calgary, Regina and Richmond. This, however, was the
only case in which someone was apprehended for the offence.

Lelas served one week in pre-trial custody. He completed his
period of imprisonment under Judge Scullion's sentence on July
12, 1990.

The respondent's co-accused, Elizabeth Major, pleaded guilty
and was given a suspended sentence. She had no prior criminal
record and showed considerable remorse for her actions. The
facts of her case are quite different, and I agree with counsel
for the Crown that disparity is not an issue in this case.

The Crown elected to proceed against Lelas by indictment. The
maximum penalty for mischief in relation to property that
exceeds $1,000 in value, if tried by indictment, is
imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years. At the
sentencing hearing, Crown counsel asked the court to impose the
maximum reformatory sentence of two years less a day. Defence
counsel suggested a sentence of 60 to 90 days with restitution
and a probation order with substantial community service.

In imposing sentence, the trial judge considered the
aggravating and mitigating factors and decided to impose a six
month concurrent sentence on each count. He was concerned that
he would make Lelas "a martyr in a white supremacy cause" if he
imposed a longer sentence. With respect, I do not understand
the learned judge's concern. The fact that Lelas may be a
martyr to those who hold similar views to his is, in my
opinion, of no consequence. He will certainly not be a martyr
to the vast majority of Canadians who do not subscribe to those
views.

In considering the fitness of the sentence imposed by the
trial judge, I wish to make it clear at the outset that Lelas
is not to be sentenced for his political or social beliefs,
repugnant as those beliefs may be. The charge is mischief, not
the promotion of hatred, and save where the beliefs of the
respondent serve to explain his actions, I do not propose to
take them into account.

As justification for the sentence imposed by the trial judge,
counsel for the respondent relied upon the following matters:

(1) Lelas pleaded guilty. This saved the Jewish community from
the further emotional upset of a trial.

(2) He apologized to the Jewish community in open court. The
pre-sentence report indicated that he realized that his actions
had not served to further his beliefs.

(3) He co-operated with the authorities by admitting his guilt,
providing a statement to the police and pleading guilty.

(4) The commission of the offences was preceded by the
ingestion of drugs and alcohol.

(5) The offences were spontaneous, unplanned and
unsophisticated. Although racist paraphernalia were discovered
in the respondent's apartment, the offences were not committed
at the instigation of any racist organization or group.

(6) The minor criminal record of the respondent.

(7) He was only 22 years of age at the time of sentencing. He
lived at home and had a good work record.

While the matters outlined by counsel for the respondent are
proper matters to be considered in determining the fitness of
the sentence imposed by the trial judge, they do not, in my
opinion, justify a six-month sentence when weighed against the
aggravating factors that exist in this case.

Whether the Jews are a racial or religious group is, in my
view, irrelevant. An offence which is directed against a
particular racial or religious group is more heinous, as it
attacks the very fabric of our society: see R. v. Ingram and
Grimsdale (1977),
1977 CanLII 2018 (ON CA)
, 35 C.C.C. (2d) 376 (Ont. C.A.), at p. 379.

This was not an isolated occurrence. As has been noted,
several similar incidents occurred within a brief period of
time following the commission of these offences. As Dubin J.A.
(as he then was) observed in R. v. Ingram and Grimsdale,
supra, such offences invite imitation and incite retaliation.

In addition, the desecration of a place of worship is a
serious matter. It is immaterial what faith is involved:
whether it is a Sikh temple, an Islamic mosque, a Jewish
synagogue or a Christian church, acts of vandalism against such
structures will not be countenanced. Such acts are rendered
more serious when they are done not just to damage the place of
worship, but, as in the present case, to cause emotional upset
and injury to the members of the congregation.

In spray painting the synagogue and Hebrew school, Lelas was
not merely intending to cause damage to property; rather, to
use his words, he wanted "to enrage the Jewish community". His
acts were done to strike fear and terror and to cause emotional
upset in the Jewish community. When mischief is racially or
religiously motivated and is done to cause emotional injury or
shock to a particular segment of Canadian society, it calls for
a far more severe penalty than mischief which is done merely to
damage property.

A sentence of six months is not, in my opinion, sufficient to
meet the needs of general deterrence and to show society's
abhorrence of the acts of the respondent. If it were not for
the fact that Lelas has been released and must be re-
incarcerated, I would have imposed a longer sentence. The
message must go out loud and clear that conduct such as that
engaged in by the respondent will not be tolerated in Canadian
society, and if it is engaged in, it will be met with a severe
penalty. Accordingly, I would allow the appeal, and increase
the sentence to one year concurrent on each count. The
probation order should stand. If the Crown requests it, a
warrant may issue for the arrest of the respondent.

GALLIGAN J.A. (dissenting):-- I agree completely with the
comments made by Houlden J.A. about the gravity of these
offences. The reprehensibleness of the respondent's conduct
cannot be overstated. It should shock the sensibilities of any
right-thinking person.

The circumstances of aggravation set out by Houlden J.A.
were, in my opinion, taken into account by the very experienced
trial judge when he imposed the sentence which he did. Were it
not for those aggravating circumstances it does not appear to
me that the offences would have called for a jail sentence of
as long as six months plus two years' probation.

Repugnant as the respondent's opinions and beliefs are, he
cannot be punished for them. I think, therefore, that a court
must ensure that a sentence could not be taken as imposing
punishment for beliefs or opinions.

It is not easy to decide upon a sentence which will express
society's abhorrence of this kind of conduct and yet not
impose, or give the appearance of imposing, punishment for the
respondent's beliefs and opinions. Arriving at a fair balance
between those two competing principles, each of which has
latent emotional impact, is a delicate exercise. It is my
opinion that the sentence which the trial judge thought
appropriate was a fair balance between them. Thus, I am of the
opinion, that there was no error in principle on his part. I am
not convinced that the sentence in all of the circumstances was
an unfit one.

Accordingly, while I would grant leave to appeal, I would
dismiss the appeal from sentence.

Application granted; appeal allowed.
